guide.title: Retirement guide
guide.subtitle: How Overview and What If work.

quick_start.title: Quick start — 5 steps
quick_start.step1_desc: In Plan inputs, set the plan type, birth month, retirement age, planning horizon, and monthly contribution.
quick_start.step2_desc: In Retirement Spending, add the monthly spending lines you want the plan to fund. Use today's money; inflation is handled by the plan assumptions.
quick_start.step3_desc: Add retirement income such as pensions, part-time work, or annuity income. For a pension fund, the estimated monthly payout uses its projected balance and configured annual payout rate unless you enter a monthly payout.
quick_start.step4_title: Check assumptions, taxes, and account shares
quick_start.step4_desc: Review projected returns, fees, volatility, inflation, withdrawal tax rates, tax buckets, and which accounts fund the goal.
quick_start.step5_title: Read Overview, then open What If
quick_start.step5_desc: Overview shows the base projection, spending coverage, and inputs. What If compares modeled market paths, stress scenarios, and assumption changes.

overview.title: Understanding Overview
overview.base_plan_desc: The hero summarizes the deterministic plan: whether spending is funded, whether the portfolio runs out before the planning horizon, and how the projected balance compares with the required capital at your target age.
overview.required_capital_desc: The estimated portfolio needed at your target age to fund the spending schedule you entered, after counting retirement income that starts later and estimated withdrawal taxes. It is a planning target, not a yearly spending rule.
overview.trajectory_desc: The solid line shows what you are projected to have. The dashed line shows what the plan is estimated to need over time. Use Today's value to read everything in today's money, or Nominal to include future inflation.
overview.coverage_desc: Your planned monthly retirement spending broken down by funding source. Income streams active at the selected retirement age appear as coloured segments; the remainder is what the portfolio must cover. Deferred streams show how the mix shifts at the age they start.
overview.input_cards_desc: The cards on the right are the editable inputs: Plan inputs, Retirement Spending, Retirement Income, Projection Assumptions, Withdrawal Taxes, and Account Shares.
overview.snapshot_desc: The table shows the projected end portfolio, yearly contribution, retirement income, planned spending, and portfolio withdrawal by age.

what_if.title: Understanding What If
what_if.market_paths_desc: We model different market paths using your assumptions. The shading shows the 10th–90th percentile range at each age; the line shows the median across paths, not an individual path. Money lasts counts paths that cover essential spending and finish with money remaining; FIRE paths must also reach financial independence.
what_if.base_case_desc: Shows the same deterministic base plan as Overview, then points to the largest stress result so you can see what matters most.
what_if.stress_tests_desc: Fixed checks show how the plan changes if returns are lower, inflation is higher, spending rises, retirement starts earlier, savings fall, or a market crash happens near retirement.
what_if.what_moves_desc: Compare savings, returns, retirement age, and spending. Green means more money left than the base plan; amber means less. Red indicates a gap or no money remaining.
what_if.crash_paths_desc: Compares a few crash-timing paths near retirement. A crash in the first retirement year can hurt more than the same crash later because withdrawals happen while the portfolio is down.

concepts.title: Key concepts
concepts.yearly_spending_desc: Your expenses drive the withdrawal. Each year the planner funds the spending plan you entered, subtracts retirement income, and estimates any tax drag on portfolio withdrawals.
concepts.target_calc_desc: The planner estimates the starting portfolio needed to fund the retirement spending schedule through the planning horizon. It models expense inflation, income timing, investment returns, fees, and withdrawal taxes. The target depends on these assumptions.
concepts.inflation_desc: The inflation assumption increases spending and inflation-linked income over time. Individual spending and income items can use their own rates.
concepts.returns_desc: Return before retirement drives accumulation. Return during retirement drives the withdrawal phase and required capital. Annual investment fees are subtracted from both. Volatility is used only in market-path checks — higher values produce a wider fan of outcomes.
concepts.horizon_desc: The age through which retirement spending and What If outcomes are modeled. This is an assumption about the planning period, not a prediction of lifespan.

italian.title: Italian retirement setup (fondo pensione, TFR, INPS)
italian.portfolio_desc: This is your main portfolio — the value Wealthfolio tracks. Set your return assumptions, fee drag, and monthly contribution here. It is the primary accumulation engine of your retirement plan.
italian.fondo_desc: Use Add pension fund. Enter its balance, contribution, assumed return, and payout start age. Estimated payout uses the configured payout rate unless you enter a monthly payout. Drawdown payments stop when the fund is depleted; annuity payments are modeled through the planning horizon.
italian.inps_desc: Use Add retirement income. Enter your estimated monthly net pension in today's money and set the payout start age. Use Indexed if you want the income to rise with the plan inflation assumption.
italian.tfr_title: TFR (Trattamento di Fine Rapporto — severance accrual)
italian.tfr_desc: If TFR is included in a pension fund, include it in the fund contribution. A separate fund can represent separate TFR savings; its modeled payout follows the configured payout rate or monthly payout.

goal.body:
The question the planner answers.

‘Retire at…’ keeps your retirement age fixed and finds the best plan for it: which account to draw from each year, how much to convert to Roth, and when to claim Social Security.

‘When can I retire?’ tries every retirement age from today to 70 and finds the earliest one where your must-have spending is covered every year for life, plus anything you want to leave behind. It takes a minute or two because each age is a full optimization.

retirement_age.body:
The age you stop working. Salary and contributions stop at the start of the year you reach this age; from then on the plan lives on savings, Social Security and other income.

This is the same retirement age used elsewhere in the goal.
retirement_age.value: An age in whole years, e.g. 62.

objective.body:
‘Fund my expenses, leave the most’ spends exactly your planned expenses each year and arranges withdrawals and taxes so the largest possible after-tax estate is left at the end.

‘Spend as much as possible’ raises all your expenses together, in the same shape, as high as the money allows while leaving at least the amount below. Your must-have spending is always covered either way.

bequest_floor.body:
The least you want to leave behind at the end of the plan, after your heirs pay income tax on inherited IRAs and 401(k)s. Use 0 if you only care about your own spending.

A higher amount lowers how much you can spend (or makes you retire later).
bequest_floor.value: A total in dollars, in today's money, e.g. 100000.

social_security_stream.body:
If your plan already has a Social Security income stream, pick it here: its start age becomes the claim age and its monthly amount the benefit at that age. It is then taxed as Social Security (at most 85% taxable) rather than as a pension.

If you have no such stream, choose ‘Enter amounts below’ and type the benefit directly.

social_security_monthly.body:
Your estimated monthly benefit if you claim at the claim age next to it, in today's money. Your personal estimate is at ssa.gov/myaccount (‘Plan for retirement’), which shows amounts for every claim age from 62 to 70.

If you let the optimizer choose the claim age, this amount is converted to your full-retirement-age benefit and adjusted for whichever age it picks.

social_security_claim_age.body:
The age you start Social Security. Claiming at 62 gives a permanently smaller check; every year you wait past full retirement age (67 for most people today) adds 8% until 70.

Use the age that matches the monthly amount you entered.

optimize_claim_age.body:
Lets the optimizer pick the claiming month between 62 and 70 instead of using the age you entered. It weighs a bigger lifelong check against drawing more from savings in the meantime, including the tax effects (waiting often leaves room for cheap Roth conversions).

It assumes you live to the end of the plan; if you expect a shorter life, an earlier claim may be wiser.

salary.body:
Your gross pay before taxes, 401(k), HSA or benefit deductions, as on your W-2 or a pay stub's year-to-date total. It is earned every year until the retirement age.

Bank deposits are take-home pay, so they understate it. Leave this empty if you no longer work.

salary_growth.body:
How fast your pay rises each year, including inflation. Equal to inflation means your pay keeps its buying power but no more; raises above inflation mean real growth.

It starts at the plan's inflation rate.

optimize_contributions.body:
When on, the optimizer decides how to split your savings while working: pre-tax 401(k), Roth 401(k), Roth IRA, HSA, or a regular brokerage account, within the yearly IRS limits and counting the employer match.

When off, you enter fixed yearly amounts instead. Pre-tax saving lowers today's tax; Roth saving lowers tax in retirement, and the optimizer compares the two for your situation.

match_rate.body:
How much your employer adds for each dollar you put into the 401(k), up to the limit next to it. 50 means 50 cents per dollar; 100 means dollar for dollar.

Your plan's summary plan description or benefits site states it, e.g. ‘50% of the first 6% of pay’.

match_cap.body: The share of your salary the match applies to. In ‘50% of the first 6% of pay’ this is 6: you get the full match by contributing at least 6% of your salary.

hsa_eligible.body:
Turn on if you are covered by a high-deductible health plan, which allows contributions to a health savings account (HSA).

HSA money goes in before tax, grows tax-free and comes out tax-free for medical costs: the best-taxed account there is, so the optimizer will usually fill it.

roth_401k_available.body: Turn on if your 401(k) lets you choose Roth (after-tax) contributions. Most plans do; check your benefits site. Off limits the optimizer to pre-tax 401(k) contributions plus a Roth IRA.

pre_tax_contribution.body:
What you put into a traditional (pre-tax) 401(k) or 403(b) each year while working. It comes out of your pay before income tax, lowering this year's tax; you pay tax when you withdraw it in retirement.

Use the yearly amount, not the percentage: for 10% of a 120,000 salary, enter 12000.

employer_contribution.body:
What your employer puts into your 401(k) each year (match plus any profit sharing). It goes into the pre-tax account and is not taxed until withdrawn.

This is a dollar amount, not a percentage: a 4% match on a 100,000 salary is 4000.

roth_contribution.body: What you put into Roth accounts (Roth 401(k) or Roth IRA) each year while working. It is taxed now but grows and comes out tax-free in retirement.

hsa_contribution.body: What you (and your employer) put into a health savings account each year while working. It is deducted before tax and can pay medical costs tax-free at any age.

taxable_contribution.body: What you invest each year in a regular (taxable) brokerage account while working, beyond retirement accounts. Any pay left over after expenses and taxes is also invested there, unless you choose to invest only part of it (with Optimize my contributions on).

state.body:
Adds state income tax to the plan. Only Virginia is modeled for now: its brackets, standard deduction, and the $12,000 age deduction from 65. Social Security is not taxed by Virginia.

Choose None if your state has no income tax.

prior_magi.body:
Your modified adjusted gross income of the last two years: adjusted gross income (Form 1040, line 11) plus tax-exempt interest (line 2a). Medicare premiums in a given year depend on income two years earlier, so these years matter once you are close to 65.

If left empty, the planner estimates it from your salary minus pre-tax 401(k) and HSA contributions.

max_roth_conversion.body:
Moving money from a traditional IRA or 401(k) to a Roth account is a Roth conversion: you pay income tax on it now, and it then grows and comes out tax-free. The optimizer converts in low-tax years, typically between retiring and starting Social Security.

Set a cap to limit the yearly amount (e.g. to keep tax bills predictable); 0 means no conversions. Leave empty for no cap.
max_roth_conversion.value: Dollars per year, e.g. 50000, or empty.

harvest_gains.body:
In years with low income, long-term capital gains can be taxed at 0%. Harvesting sells investments with gains in those years and buys them right back, so the gains are taxed at 0% and won't be taxed later.

This only matters if you have a taxable brokerage account with gains.

aca_benchmark_premium.body:
If you retire before 65, you need health insurance until Medicare. This is the yearly price of the second-lowest-cost silver plan for you on healthcare.gov (the benchmark plan). The premium tax credit lowers what you pay based on your income, and the optimizer keeps your income in check to protect it.

When you fill this in, leave health insurance out of your planned expenses so it isn't counted twice. Use 0 if you will have retiree coverage.

other_medical_expenses.body: How much of each year's spending is out-of-pocket medical costs besides insurance premiums (deductibles, copays, dental, vision), which HSA money can pay tax-free. The plan uses it only to cap tax-free HSA withdrawals (with Medicare premiums); it does not add spending. Include these costs in your spending items, such as Healthcare.

rule_of_55_balance.body:
If you leave your job in or after the year you turn 55, you can withdraw from that employer's 401(k) without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty. Enter the balance of that 401(k) (not IRAs) so the planner can use it before 59½.

Leave empty if it doesn't apply, for example if you retire before 55 or roll the 401(k) into an IRA.
rule_of_55_balance.value: A total in dollars, e.g. 300000, or empty.

sepp_start_age.body:
Substantially equal periodic payments (72(t)) let you take fixed yearly amounts from an IRA before 59½ without the 10% penalty. Once started, they must continue unchanged for 5 years or until 59½, whichever is later.

Enter the age the payments start, together with the yearly payment. Leave empty if you won't use them.

sepp_annual_payment.body: The fixed yearly amount of your 72(t) payments. IRS formulas set the maximum from your IRA balance and age; an online 72(t) calculator or your brokerage can work it out.

heirs_tax_rate.body:
The income tax rate your heirs will pay on what they inherit in traditional IRAs and 401(k)s. They must withdraw it within 10 years and pay tax at their own rate; Roth and taxable accounts pass on without income tax.

It affects how the optimizer values leaving money in pre-tax accounts versus converting it.

debts.body:
Loans such as a mortgage or car loan. Each is paid on its schedule; the optimizer can also pay extra principal when that beats investing.

If you add a loan here, leave its payment out of your planned expenses so it isn't counted twice.

debt_balance.body: What you still owe on this loan today, from your latest statement.

debt_payment.body: What you pay on this loan in a year: principal and interest, 12 times the monthly payment. Property tax and insurance held in escrow belong in your planned expenses.

markets_method.body:
Where each year's investment returns come from.

‘My projection assumptions’ uses the returns on Projection Assumptions card on the Plan tab, before and after retirement, for every account.

‘Fixed returns by asset class’ gives stocks, corporate bonds and Treasury notes a yearly return each; every account earns the blend of its own asset mix.

‘Replay market history’ uses what actually happened, year by year, starting from the year you pick: a way to test a bad sequence such as retiring in 1966 or 2000.

‘Historical average’ uses the compound average of a range of years, the same every year.

Your investment fee is taken off every return. Cash always earns inflation.

fixed_returns.body:
The yearly return of each asset class, before fees: stocks (the S&P 500 with dividends), Baa corporate bonds and 10-year Treasury notes. Cash earns inflation.

The presets are Owl's: Conservative is 6% stocks, 4% bonds, 3.3% notes with 2.8% inflation; Optimistic is 8.6%, 4.9%, 3.3% with 2.5% inflation. ‘Last 30 years’ switches to the historical average of 1996–2025.

start_year.body:
The plan's first year earns what the markets returned in this year, the next year the year after, and so on. Past 2025 it wraps around to 1928.

Years known for bad starts: 1929, 1937, 1966, 1969, 1973, 2000 and 2008.

average_range.body: The years averaged. Each asset class earns the compound (geometric) average of its returns over these years, every year of the plan.
average_range.value: Years from 1928 to 2025, at least two apart.

inflation_method.body:
With market history, inflation can come from the same years as the returns (the history's own inflation, or its average), or stay at a fixed rate.

Inflation raises your spending, tax brackets and Social Security each year, and cash earns it.

market_inflation.body: Yearly inflation for the plan. Spending, tax brackets and Social Security rise with it, and cash earns it. It starts at the Projection Assumptions' inflation.

asset_mix.body:
How each type of account is invested: the share in stocks, corporate bonds, Treasury notes and cash.

By default it comes from your holdings and their asset classes. Equity, real estate, commodities, alternatives and crypto count as stocks; fixed income is split evenly between corporate bonds and Treasury notes; holdings without an asset class count as stocks.

Turn this on to type your own mix instead, for example the mix you plan to move to.
asset_mix.value: Percent of each account type, adding up to 100.

target_mix.body: Moves every account type gradually from its starting mix to one target mix, reaching it at the age you choose and keeping it after: for example, from mostly stocks today to more bonds in retirement.
target_mix.value: Percent in each asset class, adding up to 100.

glide.body: How the mix moves toward the target. A straight line changes the same amount every year. An S-curve changes slowly at first, fastest halfway, then slowly again (Owl's S-curve).

target_age.body: The age the target mix is reached. Leave it blank to reach it at the planning horizon.

sell_current_home.body:
Sells the home you own now in the year you buy the new one. What the sale brings in, after selling costs, goes into your accounts, the loan you pick is repaid, and the current home's yearly costs stop.

The gain on a main home is assumed to fall within the $250,000 exclusion, so the sale is not taxed.

current_home_value.body: What your current home would sell for today. It grows at the new home's price growth until the sale.

selling_cost_rate.body: Agent commission, transfer taxes and other costs of selling, as a share of the sale price.

current_home_debt.body: The debt, from the Debts list below, that the sale pays off: usually the current mortgage.
current_home_debt.value: Choose one of your debts, or none.

leftover_partly.body: Leftover pay is what remains from your paychecks after spending, taxes, debt payments and contributions. When off, all of it is invested in your taxable account. When on, only the share you choose is invested and the rest is spent, which is closer to how most people actually save. A home sale's proceeds are still invested in full.

leftover_invest_rate.body: How much of each working year's leftover pay goes into your taxable account; the rest is spent. The Leftover spent column of the yearly table shows that amount.

hsa_family_coverage.body:
Turn on if your high-deductible plan covers your family, not just you. Family coverage has a higher HSA limit ($8,750 in 2026, against $4,400 for self-only).

HSA contributions are held to the limit for your coverage, plus $1,000 from 55.

tax_plan.balances_changed_up: Your account balances are up {{pct}} since this was calculated. Recalculate to plan from today's balances.
tax_plan.balances_changed_down: Your account balances are down {{pct}} since this was calculated. Recalculate to plan from today's balances.

cases.label: Case
cases.name: Name
cases.save_description: Keeps a copy of these settings and their result under a name, so you can come back and compare without recalculating.
cases.save_description_no_result: Keeps a copy of these settings under a name. They have no up-to-date result yet: run the plan first to save one with them.
cases.rename_description: Give this case a new name.
cases.will_replace: A case with this name already exists; saving replaces it.
cases.name_taken: Another case already has this name.
cases.viewing_description: A saved case is read-only. Load it into your plan to change its settings or recalculate it.
cases.no_result: This case was saved without a result. Load it into your plan and run it.
cases.load_description: This replaces your current plan settings, including your ages, spending, income and assumptions. They are not saved as a case; save them first to keep them.
cases.delete_description: The case and its saved result are removed. This cannot be undone.

home.title: {{title}}: bought in {{year}} at age {{age}}
home.note: Today's money. The down payment comes out of whichever accounts cost least in tax. The home's value is not in the after-tax estate above; it is listed here, beside it. Any mortgage left at the end is taken off the estate.

compare.title: Compare cases
compare.description: Saved cases and your current plan side by side, in today's money. Only cases saved with a result can be compared.
compare.pick_two: Pick at least two to compare.
compare.objective_differs: These cases optimize for different things (spending vs. what you leave), so their spending and estates are not like for like.
compare.no_differences: The settings are the same; only the balances they started from differ.
compare.balances_note: All accounts together at the start of each year, in today's money.
compare.empty: Comparing needs at least two plans with results: your current plan once optimized, and cases saved with a result. Save a case from the bar above.

safe_spending.title: Safe spending
safe_spending.description: The most you could spend per year (in the shape of your planned expenses) and still succeed on the share of market paths you choose. Each path is solved once for the most it can fund, so this takes about as long as the chance-of-success check.
safe_spending.running: Solving every path… this can take a few minutes.
safe_spending.not_run: No safe-spending search was saved with this case.
safe_spending.result_detail: The first-year spending at least {{rate}}% of paths fund ({{method}}, {{paths}} paths), in today's money.
safe_spending.planned: Your planned {{amount}} a year succeeds on {{rate}}% of these paths.
safe_spending.chart_note: Higher spending succeeds on fewer paths. The dashed lines mark your target rate and your planned spending. Nothing has to be left at the end; amounts include a 1% safety margin.
safe_spending.distribution_note: Each path's most first-year spending, today's money. Red marks paths that cannot fund your planned {{planned}} a year; the dashed line is your planned spending.

choices.title: What each choice costs
choices.description: Re-solves the plan with one choice changed at a time and shows how much that moves what the plan maximizes: your yearly spending, or the estate you leave. It shows where a small change buys the most.
choices.running: Re-solving the plan for each choice… about a minute.
choices.not_run: No choice costs were saved with this case.
choices.base_spending: As planned: {{amount}} a year of spending (quick solve).
choices.base_estate: As planned: an after-tax estate of {{amount}} (quick solve).
choices.minimumExpenses: need {{amount}} a year more in must-have spending
choices.conversionCap: lift the {{amount}} cap on Roth conversions
choices.claimAge: let the plan pick your Social Security age (instead of {{age}})
choices.note: Today's money. Each row changes only that one choice, using quick solves, so small differences (under about 1%) are within solver noise.

regret.title: Does this year's Roth conversion hold up?
regret.description: This year's conversion is the decision you make now; later years can adapt. This fixes this year's conversion at amounts around the recommended one, re-plans everything else on many market paths, and measures how much estate each amount gives up compared with the best amount on the same path.
regret.running: Re-solving each amount on every path… this can take several minutes.
regret.not_run: No conversion check was saved with this case.
regret.summary: Recommended this year: {{recommended}}. Least regret across {{paths}} paths: {{best}}.
regret.note: Regret is how much less after-tax estate (today's money) an amount leaves than the best amount on the same market path, with {{spending}} a year of spending held fixed. A low average and a low worst case mean the amount is a safe choice whatever markets do.

empty.title: No optimized plan yet
empty.overview: Set your plan up on the Plan tab, then optimize it. The optimized plan shows here: how much you can spend or leave, the taxes you pay, and what to do each year.
empty.risk: Optimize your plan first. This tab then tests how it holds up: its chance of success on past and resampled markets, the spending you can count on, what each choice costs, and whether this year's Roth conversion holds up.
empty.risk_infeasible: This plan has no solution, so there is nothing to test. Change its settings on the Plan tab and optimize again.

simulations.title: Monte Carlo settings
simulations.description: How many market paths each Monte Carlo check draws, from {{min}} to {{max}}. Each path re-solves your whole plan, so time grows with the count: 100 takes a few minutes, 1,000 about ten times as long. More paths give steadier percentages. Resampled years reuse whole years since 1928; lognormal draws years from a fitted distribution, so it can produce years worse (or better) than any on record.
simulations.label: Runs per check
simulations.regret_label: Runs for the Roth conversion check
simulations.lifespans_description: Instead of ending every run at your planning horizon, each Monte Carlo run draws an age at death from an actuarial table, given you live to retire at {{age}}, and plans to it. Most runs end earlier than a conservative horizon and a few run past 100, so the success rate weighs bad markets and a long life together. Historical replays and the Roth conversion check keep the horizon.

stress.title: Stress tests
stress.description: Re-solves the plan under shocks you don't control. Each time, the optimizer re-plans conversions, withdrawals and spending around the shock, as you would, and shows how much it moves what the plan maximizes.
stress.running: Re-solving the plan for each shock… about a minute.
stress.not_run: No stress tests were saved with this case.
stress.lowerReturns: returns are 2 points lower every year
stress.higherInflation: inflation is 1.5 points higher every year
stress.socialSecurityCut: Social Security pays only 77% of its promised benefit
stress.retireInto: retirement starts into the markets of {{year}}
stress.note: Today's money, using quick solves, so differences under about 1% are within solver noise. 77% is what the trustees project Social Security can pay once its trust fund runs out. The market years replay history from your first retirement year: 1929 the Depression, 1966 a decade of high inflation, 2000 two crashes.

contributions.title: Contributions while working (today's money)
contributions.none: The plan has no working years left, so there is nothing to contribute.
contributions.rerun: Optimize again to see what goes into each account; this result was solved before the breakdown existed.
contributions.capped_preTax401k: Pre-tax 401(k) is held to the IRS limit from age {{age}}; growth would take it past.
contributions.capped_roth: Roth is held to the IRS limit from age {{age}} (the 401(k) room pre-tax leaves, plus an IRA).
contributions.capped_hsa: HSA is held to the IRS limit from age {{age}}.
contributions.roth_note: Roth is the amount you entered; it can go to a Roth 401(k) or a Roth IRA.
contributions.note: Limits are 2026 dollars, raised with inflation, with catch-ups from 50 (60–63 for the 401(k)). Pay not contributed or spent goes to the taxable account (Saved in the playbook).

home_purchase.title: Home purchase
home_purchase.description: The home this goal saves for. The savings target is the down payment plus closing costs, at the price the home should have by the purchase date.
home_purchase.price_hint: Today's price; it grows with appreciation until you buy.
home_purchase.appreciation_hint: Also used for the home's value later in the Tax Plan.
home_purchase.age_needs_birth: Buying at an age needs a birth month on your retirement goal.
home_purchase.date_from_goal: Buying on {{date}}, the goal's target date.
home_purchase.date_missing: Set a target date for this goal first.
home_purchase.monthly_owning: Tax, insurance, upkeep and HOA per month
home_purchase.tax_plan_note: Saving sets this goal's target and date. A retirement plan that includes this home uses these details.

linked_home.headline: Your {{retirement}} plan pays for this home
linked_home.how_optimized: The Tax Plan takes the down payment and closing costs from the accounts that cost the least in taxes, adds the mortgage and owning costs, and stops rent from the purchase on.
linked_home.how_projection: The retirement projection takes the down payment and closing costs from your portfolio in the purchase year and adds the mortgage and owning costs to your expenses once you retire.
linked_home.incomplete: Enter the home's price and a purchase date below for the retirement plan to include it.
linked_home.run_tax_plan: Optimize the Tax Plan on your retirement goal to see which accounts pay for it.
linked_home.tax_plan_note: From the last Tax Plan run. The withdrawals cover the down payment, closing costs and that year's spending.
linked_home.tax_plan_stale: From an earlier Tax Plan run; the plan has changed since. Optimize again for current numbers.
linked_home.tax_plan_missing: The last Tax Plan run did not include this purchase. Optimize again on your retirement goal.
linked_home.projection_year_suffix: from your portfolio for the down payment and closing costs.
linked_home.projection_note: Before you retire, the mortgage and owning costs are taken to come out of your pay; from retirement on they are part of your expenses.
linked_home.projection_missing: The purchase is outside the retirement projection, or the projection is not available yet.
linked_home.funding_linked_hint: The retirement plan pays for this home from your accounts. Switch to saving with this goal's own accounts to track a savings target instead.
linked_home.funding_accounts_hint: This goal saves from its own share of your accounts. Let your retirement plan pay for it instead; this replaces any other home in that plan.
